headline: ASX closed up 0.76% on a solid Monday, but PLS took a beating — down 3.7% today — while the Middle East conflict keeps oil elevated and global markets on edge.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara dropped another 3.7% today, closing at $3.37 — it's now down 50% from your cost base. There's no specific news catalyst today, but lithium prices remain under sustained pressure globally as EV demand growth slows and new supply keeps coming online. The long-term thesis is intact but being severely tested.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two fell 2.1% in last night's US session, weighed down by fresh drama around GTA VI. A hacker known as 'Cyberleek' is threatening to leak a full playable build of GTA 6, and is taunting Take-Two with a $30M ransom demand. That's the kind of headline that spooks investors — it's a real risk to the game's commercial rollout.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE had a strong session today, up 1.7% at the close. Emerging market sentiment got a boost from a softer US dollar and some optimism around China's economy — good news for this ETF which has heavy exposure to Asian markets.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft rose 0.9% in last night's US session, bucking a slightly weaker broader market. It was one of the few big names keeping the Dow afloat while oil-price fears dragged on the S&P and Nasdaq. The AI narrative around Microsoft continues to drive investor interest heading into earnings season.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Alphabet edged up 0.6% last night. Google Cloud is reportedly growing at 82% year-on-year — a standout number — and analysts are warming to the story that Alphabet's heavy AI spending is starting to pay off. No major negative catalysts.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS gained 0.7% on the ASX today, reflecting last night's broadly mixed US session. Microsoft and a few other big names held things up, even as oil-price concerns dragged on the wider market.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG ticked up 0.43% today — a quiet, steady session for the diversified fund. No specific news. Just doing what it does: slowly grinding higher over time.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI was essentially flat today, up just 0.12%. The AI sector is in a bit of a holding pattern globally as investors digest the regulation debate heating up — particularly Microsoft's president loudly calling for rules around AI this week.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — down 50% from cost, today dropped another 3.7%
watch_today.detail: Pilbara is your biggest loss by far — you're down $75 on a $150 investment. Today's drop to $3.37 has no single catalyst but reflects the ongoing lithium price slump. The long-term EV/lithium thesis is still alive, but this is a slow grind. For a buy-and-hold investor, selling now locks in the loss at the worst possible moment. Sit tight unless your conviction in the lithium thesis has fundamentally changed.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA 6 leaker threatening full game dump
watch_today.detail: Take-Two fell 2.1% last night and the headline is ugly: a hacker calling themselves 'Cyberleek' is threatening to release a full playable build of GTA 6 unless Take-Two pays $30M. This is a real business risk — if a leak circulates widely before launch, it could dampen sales momentum. That said, GTA 6 is one of the most anticipated games ever and a leak is unlikely to kill it. You're already down 10% overall. For a long-term holder, the thesis is still a blockbuster GTA 6 launch. Hold, but watch how this develops.

watch_today.title: Oil spiking — watch inflation & rate cut hopes
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) jumped over 2% last night to $93.72 a barrel, driven by escalating Middle East conflict. Higher oil means higher fuel and transport costs, which feeds into inflation — and inflation is the enemy of interest rate cuts. If oil stays elevated, the RBA (and the US Fed) will be slower to cut rates. Watch this one carefully this week.

watch_today.title: MSFT — strong momentum heading into earnings season
watch_today.detail: Microsoft rose last night and is one of the standout performers in your portfolio, up 21.8% from your cost base. The AI story remains strong, the Microsoft president is dominating headlines on AI regulation (keeping the brand front of mind), and earnings season is approaching. No reason to change anything — this is working.

watch_today.title: VGE.AX — best mover today, up 1.7%
watch_today.detail: Your Emerging Markets ETF had a great session today. Emerging markets are benefiting from a stable AUD and some China optimism. Still only slightly in the green overall (+0.58% total return), but the trend today is encouraging. Long-term hold — no action needed.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cut hopes fading — new report pours cold water
watch_today.detail: A fresh report today suggests interest rate cuts in Australia may be further away than markets had hoped, with mortgage burdens already at levels not seen since 1989. Higher-for-longer rates are a headwind for growth stocks and property. Keep this in mind for your broader portfolio — it's not a reason to sell anything, but good context.

world.summary: The Middle East conflict continues to dominate global headlines, with Iran rejecting the latest US ceasefire proposal and oil prices surging as a result. Separately, global growth is slowing, the US is fighting over taxpayer-funded political ads, and Mike Pence is claiming victory while warning the fight isn't over.

stories.title: Iran rejects US ceasefire proposal as Middle East conflict drags on
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has officially called the latest US proposal to end the Middle East war 'insufficient', meaning peace talks are stalling. Meanwhile, Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial in Israel has resumed, adding domestic political pressure on the Israeli PM while the conflict rages. With no ceasefire in sight, the war looks set to continue — and that has direct flow-on effects for global oil prices and inflation everywhere, including Australia.

stories.title: Middle East war is 'spiralling beyond America's control', analysts warn
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple analysts are now saying the US-involved Middle East conflict has grown beyond what Washington can control or contain. The war, originally framed as a targeted campaign, has expanded in scope and drawn in more regional players. For everyday people, this matters because broader conflicts mean higher energy costs, more global uncertainty, and greater risk of the kind of economic disruption that hits supply chains and petrol prices.

stories.title: Oil surges 2% — both Middle East and Ukraine wars driving diesel prices higher
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil jumped over 2% last night to $93.72 a barrel — a big single-day move. The BBC is reporting that both the Middle East conflict and the ongoing Ukraine war are contributing to rising diesel prices, as both regions are major players in the global energy market. Higher diesel means higher costs for trucking, farming, and manufacturing — which eventually show up in the price of groceries and goods at the shops.

stories.title: US judge orders Trump administration to halt taxpayer-funded TV ads
stories.why_it_matters: A US federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately stop running government-funded TV ads — ruling that using taxpayer money to effectively run political advertising is improper. It's a significant legal check on executive power and adds to growing legal battles surrounding the current US administration. Political instability in the US is always worth watching because it affects global market confidence.

stories.title: Global economic growth slows to 2.6%, raising alarm bells
stories.why_it_matters: The global economy is growing at just 2.6% — a slowdown that is ringing alarm bells for economists. That's below the 3%+ rate considered healthy. When global growth slows, demand for Australian commodity exports like iron ore, coal, and lithium weakens, which is bad for the ASX mining sector and puts pressure on the Aussie dollar. The Institute for Fiscal Studies is also separately warning of 'headwinds on the horizon' for major economies.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 had a solid Monday, closing up 0.76% to 8,783. Meanwhile last night in the US, the S&P 500 slipped 0.1% and the Nasdaq fell 0.4% — oil jumping 2% on Middle East tensions was the main culprit, as higher oil prices stoke inflation fears and dampen rate-cut hopes. Gold pulled back 0.7%. The Aussie dollar was essentially flat at 69.6 US cents.

politics.summary: Australian politics today is dominated by two big themes: the mortgage pain crisis reaching 1989-era levels, and serious doubts being cast on when (or whether) the RBA will cut interest rates. There's also a push to regulate Big Tech algorithms.

stories.title: Mortgage burden hits worst levels since 1989 as rate rise pain bites hard
stories.why_it_matters: The AFR is reporting that Australian mortgage holders are now carrying a debt burden as severe as during the 1989 recession — one of the worst economic periods in modern Australian history. Relentless rate rises have pushed monthly repayments to levels most homeowners haven't experienced in their lifetimes. For renters, landlords passing on costs means rent isn't getting any cheaper either. This is the real-world pain that the RBA's rate decisions are causing for everyday Australians.

stories.title: New report pours cold water on rate cut expectations
stories.why_it_matters: A new economic report today is throwing cold water on hopes that the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) will cut interest rates soon. Markets had been expecting cuts, but rising oil prices, sticky inflation, and global headwinds are making the RBA's job harder. With the RBA next meeting soon, anyone with a variable rate mortgage or investment loan should temper their expectations. There's also a separate warning today about politicians trying to interfere with the RBA's independence — which economists say would be dangerous.

stories.title: Almost 80,000 older Australians expected to drop private health insurance over reforms
stories.why_it_matters: Up to 80,000 older Australians are expected to drop their private health insurance as a result of upcoming government changes to the private health system. That's a significant number — and it puts more pressure on the already-strained public hospital system. For anyone holding private health insurance, it's worth watching whether your premium and benefits change as insurers adjust to a shrinking older customer base.

stories.title: Labor wants algorithm changes passed; Greens want power to sue Big Tech
stories.why_it_matters: The Labor government wants to push through legislation changing how social media algorithms work — essentially forcing platforms to be more transparent about what content they serve users. The Greens are pushing further, wanting Australians to have the legal right to sue Big Tech companies for harm caused by their algorithms. These reforms would be significant for companies like Meta, Google, and TikTok operating in Australia — and could set a precedent for other countries.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the big theme today — Microsoft's president is making global headlines saying AI is less regulated than milk, and Britain is positioning itself as the world's AI regulation leader following a US policy shift.

stories.title: Microsoft president: 'AI is less regulated than milk'
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft president Brad Smith made waves today by publicly stating that artificial intelligence is currently less regulated than milk — pointing out that dairy products face strict safety rules, but AI systems shaping elections, healthcare, and finance do not. Smith was speaking in the UK, where he said Britain is best placed globally to lead on AI governance. It's a striking quote that's gaining traction and could accelerate pressure on governments worldwide to act.

stories.title: Britain to get first look at new AI systems after White House U-turn
stories.why_it_matters: Following a policy reversal from the White House, Britain has been granted early access to preview new AI systems before they are publicly released — making the UK the first country outside the US to receive such access. This gives British regulators and safety researchers a head-start in understanding the capabilities and risks of powerful new AI models. It's a significant diplomatic and tech-policy win for the UK.

stories.title: UK minister: AI regulation should mirror laws from the Industrial Revolution
stories.why_it_matters: A UK government minister is arguing that AI needs to be regulated in the same phased, practical way that factory safety laws were introduced during the Industrial Revolution — starting with the most dangerous applications and expanding from there. The analogy is interesting: back then, child labour laws and workplace safety rules didn't kill the industrial boom, they made it more sustainable. The minister is pushing back against those who say any AI regulation will stifle innovation.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters beat the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. The Rugby League World Cup is now front of mind, the AFL trade period is heating up, and there's drama around Bulldogs forward Xerri's exit.

stories.title: Roosters win 2026 NRL Grand Final over Knights 19-18
stories.why_it_matters: It was a one-point thriller at Accor Stadium — the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 to claim the 2026 NRL premiership. Doesn't get much tighter than that. The Knights came agonisingly close but the Roosters held on in what was reportedly a gripping final.

stories.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Full schedule and how it works
stories.why_it_matters: With the NRL season wrapped up, attention is quickly turning to the 2026 Rugby League World Cup. Fox Sports has published the full schedule and a guide to how the tournament works. The Kangaroos (Australia's national team) are among the favourites, and team tips are already circulating — including a 'bombshell' fullback selection call and a controversial young prodigy cleared to play.

stories.title: Xerri opens up on 'brutal' Bulldogs exit: 'Who leaked it?'
stories.why_it_matters: Bulldogs forward Nicho Hynes — wait, it's Xerri — has spoken out publicly about his exit from the Canterbury Bulldogs, calling it 'brutal' and asking 'who leaked it?' about the way his departure became public. The interview suggests there's bad blood over how the club handled his exit. A messy off-season saga for the Bulldogs just as they're trying to rebuild.

stories.title: AFL trade period: Roos improve offer for Blakey, Blues chase Giant, Cats forward to stay
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL trade period is in full swing. North Melbourne has improved their offer for Hawks midfielder James Blakey. Carlton is continuing to chase a Greater Western Sydney player. And a Geelong forward who was expected to be traded has reportedly decided to stay at the club. The Hawthorn Hawks are also being analysed for how they handle their star-studded forward line depth going into 2027.
